query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive model based on geometric deep learning (e.g., an E(3)NN approach) will correctly identify high-entropy alloys with exceptionally low phonon thermal conductivity by directly incorporating the full 3D atomic configurations and crystallographic symmetries into its prediction of the phonon density of states and derived thermal properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline high-entropy alloys (e.g., GeTe-based or PbSe-based chalcogenide HEAs) with complex, multi-element atomic distributions.
generation.intervention: Application of the E(3)NN-based predictive model to calculate the phonon density of states and related parameters (e.g., Debye temperature, dominant phonon wavelength) for HEAs.
generation.conditions: Ambient to high temperatures (where thermal insulation performance is critical), using HEAs with well-characterized crystalline structures.
generation.structural_mediator: The model leverages the accurate geometric representation of atomic arrangements and inherent crystallographic symmetry, which mediate the phonon scattering processes responsible for low lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.mechanism: By preserving 3D translational, rotational, and inversion symmetries, the E(3)NN efficiently extracts features from the atomic-scale structure that correlate with phonon scattering events (driven by mass disorder and strain fluctuations), leading to more accurate predictions of the phonon density of states and, consequently, the lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will outperform traditional prediction methods (e.g., discrete point prediction or virtual crystal approximations) by achieving at least a 20-30% improvement in predictive accuracy for lattice thermal conductivity in HEAs, thereby reliably identifying materials with ultra-low phonon thermal conductivity.
generation.baseline: Existing methods that either rely on limited discrete property estimates or approximations such as the VCA, which may fail to capture the complex interplay of multi-element disorder and symmetry in HEAs.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be effective primarily for crystalline HEAs with well-defined atomic positions; its reliability may diminish for amorphous or poorly characterized systems and for compositions far outside the training data domain.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the availability and quality of training data for very complex or novel HEA compositions, which might limit the model’s accuracy. Additionally, real-world experimental conditions could introduce factors (e.g., defects, grain boundaries) not fully captured by the model.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of high-entropy alloy samples that the predictive model identifies as having exceptionally low lattice thermal conductivity. Characterize their phonon density of states using inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering and measure their lattice thermal conductivity using standardized thermal transport techniques.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if, for a statistically significant number of the model-selected HEAs, the experimentally measured lattice thermal conductivity deviates by more than 25% from the predicted values, or if the phonon density-of-states profiles do not exhibit the characteristic shifts (e.g., reduced dominant phonon wavelengths) associated with enhanced phonon scattering.

## Abstract
GeTe-based and PbSe-based high-entropy compounds have outstanding thermoelectric (TE) performance and crucial applications in mid and high temperatures. Recently, the optimization of TE performance of high-entropy compounds has been focused on reducing thermal conductivity by strengthening the phonon scattering process to improve TE performance. We report a first-principles investigation on nine GeTe-based high-entropy chalcogenide solid solutions constituted of eight metallic elements (Ag, Pb, Sb, Bi, Cu, Cd, Mn, and Sn) and 13 PbSe-based high-entropy chalcogenide solid solutions: Pb0.99-ySb0.012SnySe1-2xTexSx (x = 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, 0.3, 0.35, 0.4, 0.45, and y = 0) and Pb0.99-ySb0.012SnySe1-2xTexSx (y = 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25 and x = 0.25). We have investigated the mechanical properties focusing on Debye temperature (ΘD), thermal conductivity (κ), Grüneisen parameter (γα), dominant phonon wavelength (λdom), and melting temperature (Tm). We find that the lattice thermal conductivity is significantly reduced when GeTe is alloyed into the following compositions: Ge0.75Sb0.13Pb0.12Te, Ge0.61Ag0.11Sb0.13Pb0.12Bi0.01Te, and Ge0.61Ag0.11Sb0.13Pb0.12Mn0.05Bi0.01Te. However, the prediction of continuous properties from limited input information remains challenging due to the output complexity and finite data volume. Moreover, for crystalline solids, the crystallographic symmetry poses additional constraints on a generic neural network.
In this work, we build a ML‐based predictive model that directly outputs the phonon density of states (DoS) using atomic structures as input.
